paragraphs: The following judgments address the daily work of mechanical drafters who use CAD to draw and revise mechanical drawings; they do not predict hiring, qualifications, authorization, or engineering and technical safety responsibility.

The core of a mechanical drafter's work is using CAD software to turn concepts for machinery and mechanical devices into manufacturable detailed drawings: building three-dimensional models, drawing schematic, orthographic, and angular views, annotating dimensions, tolerances, and fastening methods, compiling bills of materials, and revising drawings in response to design changes or production problems. The work is mainly indoors, with long periods of sitting and computer operation, and it emphasizes precision and version consistency.

A fully fictional task package: given a fictional mechanical part design input (containing 1 set of functional and assembly requirements, 1 set of fictional dimensions and tolerance ranges, and 1 fastening and fit example to be judged), write within 60 minutes the modeling and drawing steps, the dimensions and tolerances that need to be annotated, the key points of the bill of materials, and the situations that need to be confirmed with an engineer; do not use real clients, enterprise data, or unpublished drawings of others.

Sample output and reflection: check whether the functional and assembly requirements are verified first, whether the order of modeling, views, and annotation is explained, whether the basis for dimensions and tolerances is given, and whether the three kinds of problems of geometry, process, and version are distinguished; then ask yourself whether you can stay focused on computer drafting for long periods, whether you can check details against standards, and whether you are willing to confirm with an engineer first when uncertain.

This page covers O*NET 17-3013.00 "Mechanical Drafters": preparing detailed working drawings of machinery and mechanical devices, including dimensions, fastening methods, and other engineering information; common job titles include CAD designer, CAD operator, design drafter, drafting technician, and mechanical designer. The work is mainly indoors, in a controlled environment, with long periods of computer drafting. This page does not cover adjacent occupations such as architectural and civil drafters (17-3011.00) and electrical and electronics drafters (17-3012.00).

entries: Inputs: functional and assembly requirements of machinery and mechanical devices, sketches and existing drawings, dimensions and tolerances, materials and fastening methods, BOM and version rules, CAD/CAM software and three-dimensional models, and engineering and manufacturing standards.

Checkable outputs: three-dimensional models with dimensions and tolerances, schematic and orthographic views, fully annotated part and assembly drawings, bills of materials, drawing versions revised per feedback, and design notes and change records that can be handed over.

Complete workflow: verify functional and assembly requirements → collect sketches, specifications, and existing drawings → build a three-dimensional model → draw schematic and orthographic views and annotate dimensions and tolerances → compile the bill of materials → revise and archive versions per review and production feedback, in a closed loop.

paragraphs: Work reality: 100% of O*NET respondents work indoors in a controlled environment every day, 47% sit continuously, 78% use email daily, 65% collaborate face to face daily, and 56% report a typical 40-hour week; these are United States respondent situations, not all jobs. Verify engineering intent, dimensions and tolerances, views, BOM, and versions, and hand uncertain items to an engineering reviewer with clearly defined responsibility for confirmation.

Environment and pace: the work is mainly in an indoor controlled environment (about 100% indoors every day), with long periods of sitting (about 47% continuously or almost continuously) and repetitive computer work (about 42% continuously or almost continuously), and daily collaboration mainly by email (about 78%) and face-to-face discussion (about 65%); about 56% report a standard work week of 40 hours, and precision and accuracy are important.

Research inputs: 17-3013 tasks, context, RCI, education, and JobZone; 2025 wages and 2025—2035 projections. Mechanical drafting sub-items and the drafting group are counted separately, and the United States catalog does not prove Chinese qualifications or industry placement.

What to verify first: functional and assembly requirements, sketches and existing drawings, dimensions and tolerances, materials and fastening methods, BOM and version rules, and the engineering judgments that need engineer confirmation.

Work loop: starting from verifying functional and assembly requirements, going through building a three-dimensional model, drawing views and annotating dimensions and tolerances, and compiling the bill of materials, to revising and archiving versions per review and production feedback; do not produce drawings before all requirements and tolerances are confirmed, and do not deliver before all inconsistencies between drawings and the BOM are corrected.

On this page, mechanical drafting is separated from architectural and civil drafting and electrical and electronics drafting by subject matter and tasks; engineering decisions, review, and sign-off depend on the specific jurisdiction and employer responsibilities, and the O*NET catalog does not imply that mechanical engineers generally hold exclusive sign-off authority.

Difference from architectural and civil drafters (17-3011.00): they work on architectural and civil structural drawings, while this occupation works on mechanism, part, and assembly drawings for machinery and mechanical devices.

Difference from electrical and electronics drafters (17-3012.00): they work on electrical and electronic schematic and wiring drawings, while this occupation works on mechanical dimensions, tolerances, and fastening.

Difference from commercial and industrial designers (27-1021.00): designers are responsible for appearance and usability concepts, while mechanical drafters turn an already defined concept into manufacturable technical drawings.

Difference from machinists: machinists machine parts to drawings, while mechanical drafters are responsible for drawings and modeling; before choosing this occupation, compare actual tasks, standards, authorization, and growth paths, and do not decide based on title similarity.

Task ability: AI task exposure for mechanical drafters is not equal to job replacement: CAD software and generative tools can assist with modeling, drawing output, and retrieval, but judging engineering intent, deciding tolerances and fastening, review sign-off, and final delivery still need to be handled by people.

Editorial suggestion: pilot description drafting, version comparison, BOM proofreading, and standards retrieval; the original task materials describe CAD modeling and do not prove that generative tools reliably produce drawings or have been adopted. Evaluate against actual error records, and do not automatically release engineering decisions. AI Impact Score 67% is an editorial estimate. Model impact index for three equally weighted representative core tasks; not a measured share of working time or a job-loss probability. floor((75+75+50)/3+0.5)=67; fermatmind-ai-impact-v1; 2026-10-18.The three tasks, ratings and sources are listed in the FermatMind method source record on this page.

Data and system thresholds: before adoption, verify the models, drawings, BOM, and version data in the CAD/PDM system, whether permissions and auditing are complete, and the failure modes of tool output against manufacturing standards; engineering judgment cannot rely on software output alone.

Human control: tolerances and fits, fastening and material selection, whether something is manufacturable, and whether a version is issued must be reviewed by drafters and engineers according to their responsibilities; software output does not constitute design sign-off.

Remaining responsibility: must not be released automatically: engineering intent judgment, drawing sign-off, design changes, and final delivery. Output from any tool or system is not equal to an authorization conclusion.

Failure risk: if software or automatically generated output is not reviewed, it may introduce dimension or tolerance errors and inconsistencies between views and the BOM, causing rework, scrap, or assembly failure.

Employment evidence boundaries: the available materials are mainly task-level exposure research (such as the ILO 2025 generative AI exposure index), and they cannot be used to infer adoption rates, job cuts, or a timeline for this occupation; task exposure, adoption, productivity, and employment are different measurement targets.

Before the editorial pilot, verify CAD/PDM versions and BOM and model permissions; the human control of material and version management is cross-checking the consistency of drawings, models, and the BOM and releasing through the process, not replacing it with automatic output.

This page does not obtain a national occupational wage median for mechanical drafters in mainland China. The NBS2025 annual average for the manufacturing industry is used only as employer background for manufacturing enterprises; enterprises such as design services should verify against their actual industry, and United States classifications are not mapped uniformly onto Chinese industries.

All are industry scopes and are not equal to the median or starting pay for this occupation.

Insufficient evidence: no national occupational wage median for mechanical drafters in mainland China was obtained (2025 official public scope); this page only presents the manufacturing industry proxy and marks it as an industry scope, and does not fill the gap with proxy numbers or United States figures.
United States mechanical drafters: 2025 wages, 2025—2035 projections

United States 17-3013: 2025 annual wages P10/P25/P50/P75/P90 are 48,360 / 58,080 / 71,550 / 86,120 / 106,580 USD, and hourly 23.25 / 27.93 / 34.40 / 41.41 / 51.24 USD. Employment of 42,100 in 2025 and a projected 39,600 in 2035, a decline of 6% and a net decrease of 2,500, with 2,900 average annual openings including replacements. Percentiles are not seniority, and the projections are not AI attribution.

Wage statistical position: the figures above are a statistical distribution under the United States national scope; percentiles do not represent seniority or experience levels, and average annual openings include replacement demand and are not equal to the number of advertised positions or an individual's probability of being hired.

How to understand these positions: percentiles are points in a statistical distribution, not promotion levels; employment change (a decline in this case) and average annual openings are different indicators and cannot substitute for each other; industry and regional differences are large and must not be extrapolated across regions.

Current O*NET United States industry distribution for this occupation is manufacturing 50%, professional, scientific, and technical services 22%, construction 10%, and other 18%; no sub-occupation industry wages were obtained. The combined BLS drafting group industry wages must not be used to fill in mechanical drafting.

2025—2035: mechanical drafting from 42,100 to 39,600, a decline of 6% and a net decrease of 2,500; the 2,900 average annual openings include replacements, so the decline must not be equated with there being no openings, and it is not proof that generative AI caused the decline.
Task signal: able to stay focused on computer drafting for long periods and to check dimensions and tolerances against standards, keeping drawings precise and versions consistent.
Task signal: able to turn functional and assembly requirements into views and annotations, and to explain design intent and limits.
Task signal: able to find inconsistencies between drawings and the BOM or versions and correct them proactively.

Big Five is only for self-reflection; editorial observations suggest checking whether you can review dimensions, tolerances, the BOM, and versions item by item and proactively report uncertain engineering intent, without treating detail labels as validity for this occupation or as sign-off qualification.

Caution conditions: if it is hard to stay focused on screen details for long periods, or you lack patience for repeated revisions and version management, you may first compare adjacent directions or on-site roles.

Caution conditions: interest assessments for mechanical drafters are for exploration only and still require verification of real tasks, environment, qualifications, and learning costs; they cannot determine competence or qualification.
Trial action: complete one modeling, drawing, and BOM exercise using a fully fictional part design input, and ask someone else to review the dimensions and tolerances.
RIASEC or personality frameworks can only help raise questions and cannot replace work samples, learning ability, qualifications, and actual performance evidence for mechanical drafters.

Dimension and tolerance errors: when drawings are not checked against functional and assembly requirements, the trigger is a wrong key dimension or tolerance annotation; it may lead to scrapped parts or assembly failure; the control is to review dimensions, tolerances, and fits against standards and confirm with an engineer; the boundary is set by engineering standards and employer requirements.

Incomplete views and annotations: when producing drawings, necessary views or annotations are omitted, with the trigger being that views, sections, and annotations were not organized per drafting standards; it may cause manufacturing ambiguity or rework; the control is to check the completeness of views and annotations against a standard checklist.

Drawings inconsistent with the bill of materials: when compiling the BOM, the trigger is that part numbers, quantities, or specifications do not match the drawings; it may cause procurement and production errors; the control is to cross-check drawings against the BOM and record the version.

Versions and changes not synchronized: during design changes, the trigger is that an old version is still in circulation or the change was not recorded; it may cause manufacturing to work from an old drawing; the control is to release the new version through the change process and withdraw old versions.

Common escalation rule: once engineering intent, applicability of standards, or version ownership is unclear, stop producing or delivering drawings first, and hand the facts, impact, and open questions to the engineering lead for confirmation before continuing.

Realistic entry point: entry samples for mechanical drafters use only public or fictional data, demonstrating modeling, drawing, annotation, and BOM records; first confirm the first-year tasks and the engineering review method of the target position.

The United States BLS drafting group generally requires postsecondary drafting education, usually two years, and there are also certificate and diploma routes; the O*NET figures for this sub-item of 44% high school, 23% two-year, and 19% bachelor's degree are respondent feedback, not shares of jobs. The general 1—2 years of training in JobZone3 is not a fixed number of years for this occupation. Materials on the corresponding Chinese qualifications and sign-off system have not yet been established and must be verified against the target position.

No-experience work sample: one fully fictional part design input; within 60 minutes write the modeling and drawing steps, the basis for dimensions and tolerances, the key points of the BOM, and the situations that need engineer confirmation, without using real client and enterprise data.

Education, professional certification, institutional appointment, and design sign-off authority are separate; BLS states that drafting certification is not mandatory, but that does not mean all jurisdictions waive qualifications. Specific design responsibility in China depends on the competent system and unit procedures, and where these have not been obtained, a uniform exemption is not presumed.

Seven-day trial: on the first two days understand the functional requirements and drafting standards, over the middle three days complete one fictional part modeling and drawing exercise, on the sixth day ask someone else to challenge the dimensions and tolerances, and on the seventh day write down the evidence for continuing, stopping, or changing direction.

Qualification decisions: the O*NET mechanical drafter certification and apprenticeship directories are used to discover possible certificates and apprenticeship opportunities, but certification is not equal to a license, employer appointment, or design sign-off authority; certificates, hiring, and sign-off responsibility are different statuses.

Ability ladder: before entering mechanical drafting, verify the official occupation scope, real employer requirements, education or training, local qualifications, and supervised tasks, and do not infer directly from the conditions of adjacent occupations; advancement is based on reviewable drawings and reviews, not guaranteed years.

Transition path: before transitioning, list transferable abilities (CAD modeling, drafting standards, BOM and version management) and the engineering, material, and process knowledge that must be filled in, and verify item by item against the qualifications and responsibilities of adjacent positions.

United States mechanical drafting currently stands at 42,100 employed in 2025 and a projected 39,600 in 2035, a decline of 6% and a net decrease of 2,500 from 2025 to 2035; the 2,900 average annual openings include replacements, and the overall projection is not AI attribution.
Employment numbers, growth rate, net change, and annual openings must be explained separately and cannot be combined into a personal employment guarantee.

Architectural and civil drafting requires filling in architectural structures and civil objects, elevations and discipline interfaces, and the corresponding standards; verify training, drawing review, and authority against the employer and jurisdiction, as it is not an automatic transfer.

career_risk_cards.heading: Work risks and boundaries of mechanical drafters

risks.consequence: May lead to scrapped parts or assembly failure.
risks.mitigation: Review tolerances and fits against standards and confirm with an engineer.
risks.scenario: Annotating key dimensions or tolerances without verifying functional and assembly requirements.

risks.consequence: May cause manufacturing ambiguity or rework.
risks.mitigation: Check the completeness of views and annotations against a standards checklist.
risks.scenario: Omitting necessary views, sections, or annotations when producing drawings.

risks.consequence: May cause procurement and production errors.
risks.mitigation: Cross-check drawings against the BOM and record the version.
risks.scenario: Numbers, quantities, or specifications not matching the drawings when compiling the bill of materials.

risks.consequence: May cause losses from working to an old drawing.
risks.mitigation: Release the new version through the change process and withdraw the old version.
risks.scenario: An old version still in circulation or a change not recorded during a design change.

risks.consequence: May cause erroneous drawings or delayed delivery.
risks.mitigation: Stop producing drawings first and hand the matter to the engineering lead for confirmation.
risks.scenario: Engineering intent, applicability of standards, or version ownership is unclear.

risks.consequence: May cause mismatches in standards and responsibility.
risks.mitigation: Distinguish adjacent positions using the O*NET scope.
risks.scenario: Confusing this occupation with architectural drafters, electrical drafters, or machinists.

subject.name: Mechanical drafters
subject.summary: Mechanical drafters (O*NET 17-3013.00) use CAD software to turn concepts for machinery and mechanical devices into detailed working drawings containing dimensions, fastening methods, and engineering information: building three-dimensional models, drawing schematic and orthographic views, compiling bills of materials, and revising designs per feedback.
